title: "The self is to be seen, heard, reflected on" (2.4)
hook: the second half of Yajnavalkya's sentence, and the four verbs a whole school of philosophy is built on
carry: for the sake of the self
tomorrow: the lump of salt dissolved — no inside, no outside

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maitreyi set aside the whole earth full of wealth and asked for what doesn't die. Yajnavalkya began: not for the husband's sake is a husband dear. What in one of your loves wasn't really about them? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

Try catching a drumbeat. Not the drum: the sound. Reach into the air after it's struck and grab the boom. You can't. It's gone before your hand closes. But put your hand on the drum, or on the drummer's arm, and you've got every sound it will ever make. Yajnavalkya uses exactly that picture, in the middle of his talk with Maitreyi. Yesterday he took love apart: not for the husband's sake. Today he finishes the sentence, and tells her where to put her hand.
screen: `TRY CATCHING A DRUMBEAT.` → `HOLD THE DRUM INSTEAD.` → `WHERE TO PUT YOUR HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sentence. Not for the husband's sake is a husband dear, but for the sake of the self a husband is dear. Not for the wife's sake, but for the sake of the self. And so on through sons, wealth, gods, all beings, everything. Every love you've ever had, he says, is lit from one place. Then the line this day is named for: atma va are drashtavyah shrotavyo mantavyo nididhyasitavyah. The self, my dear, is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected on, to be meditated on, Maitreyi. And when the self is seen, heard, reflected on and understood, all this is known. That's where the drum comes in. You can't catch the sounds one by one. Hold the drum, or the drummer, and the sounds are held. He gives two more: the conch, and the vina, a stringed instrument. Know the source, and you know what comes from it. Centuries later, teachers of Vedanta built a whole method on these four verbs. Shravana: hearing the teaching, really listening. Manana: reflecting, turning it over, answering your own doubts. Nididhyasana: dwelling in it, steadily, until it's not an idea any more. And seeing, which comes first in the sentence, many of them read as the goal, the thing the other three are for. Notice the order. Listen first. Think second. Sit with it third. It's a fair description of what you've been doing on this path, every day, for a year.
screen: `FOR THE SAKE OF THE SELF.` · `SEEN, HEARD, REFLECTED, MEDITATED ON.` · `HOLD THE DRUM, AND THE SOUND IS HELD.` · `SHRAVANA, MANANA, NIDIDHYASANA.` · then, large: `KNOW THE SELF, AND ALL THIS IS KNOWN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, in the three steps. Hear: say the line quietly to yourself once. For the sake of the self. Reflect: let one question come about it, any question, and turn it over for a few breaths without forcing an answer. Then dwell: drop the words, and simply rest where they were pointing, the place you're hearing and thinking from. When thoughts come back, start again at hearing. The bell holds the time.
Nididhyasana. Deep, steady contemplation: the third step after hearing and reflecting, when the teaching stops being an idea and starts being lived.
Your line: for the sake of the self. Today, take one thing you heard this week and give it a minute of reflection, then a minute of quiet. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: In Vedanta study, students follow the three steps drawn from this verse: shravana, hearing the teaching from a teacher; manana, reflecting on it and resolving doubts; and nididhyasana, sustained contemplation.

match.prompt: the three steps — tap the pairs.
pairs: hold it, and the sound is held

myth: the four verbs are seen, heard, reflected on, meditated on
Yajnavalkya says you can catch a drum's sounds one by one
you can't. hold the drum or the drummer, and the sounds are held.
"for the sake of the self" means love is selfish
every love is lit from the self at the center; that's the source, not a motive.

fork.setup: you want to know the self, Vedanta-style. what comes first?
fork.reveal: hearing, shravana. then reflecting, manana. then dwelling in it, nididhyasana. many teachers read the seeing as where the three lead.

original.note: Sanskrit nididhyāsana: from dhyai, to meditate, in a form meaning to want to dwell on it steadily.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about looking inward.
what it means: every love is lit from the self, so the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on, and then all this is known.
what a scholar hears: 2.4.5 became the root of Vedanta's three disciplines, shravana, manana, nididhyasana, with the seeing read as the goal.

sources.quoted: atma va are drashtavyah shrotavyo mantavyo nididhyasitavyah

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.7–9 (the drum, the conch, the vina)

notes: The index word is the title's head cut at the comma ("The self is to be seen); kept exactly. The word screen shows nididhyasana instead.
Sanskrit given without diacritics: ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyo maitreyi. Confirm.
Shravana/manana/nididhyasana as a three-step method is especially Advaita's (Shankara and later); 'seeing as the goal' reflects Shankara's reading. Confirm the phrasing 'many of them'.
The drum (dundubhi), conch (śaṅkha) and vina images: 2.4.7–9; confirm.
The etymology note on nididhyāsana (desiderative of dhyai) should be checked.
